raw_comment: Economic stagnation yields a less favorable market for fast food. I notice that the wealthiest nations are among the most middling data points, implying that as countries reach the highest wealth echelon, their economic growth slows. This slowed growth yields stability, allowing a booming middle class that then allows individuals access to more expensive (and often healthier) food options. During this transitional phase, the lower class is, for the first time, gaining access to greater diversity of food options, maybe even having the option to purchase food rather than grow it for the first time. Additionally, these nations often have massive metropolitan centers rife with poverty, a market environment perfect for the fast food sector to corner.

raw_comment:
Not only are fast-food sales increasing in the United Sates, but also eating fast food is a life-style change that is being exported to countries around the world.  With more fast-food sales and more wealth, there are some unintended consequences that you may not have thought about until now.  View the Reveal tomorrow afternoon and see where the article took this data in explaining what is happening to new customers.
Jesse of Brooklyn had an interesting headline “Fast Food Preys on the Poor.” Discuss with your class whether there is evidence of this in the graph or do you have other knowledge that supports this headline.
Thanks to all teachers and students who responded.  You can continue to post responses. Dig deeper into what the graph shows. Please check back on Thursday afternoon, October 18 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graphs, and three Stat Nuggets. 

Next week’s graph will be released TOMORROW – THURSDAY OCTOBER 18! You may respond before the live moderation on Wednesday, October 24, during the moderation, or after the moderation by going to the archives for the graph.  No surprise – the graph has to do with the upcoming midterm elections and the barriers to voting by state.   Signing off – Sharon Hessney in Boston and Jared Derksen in Rancho Cucamonga, California. 

NOTE:  There will be no “What’s Going On In This Graph?” on Wednesday, October 31.  Happy Halloween.

raw_comment: Economic stagnation yields a less favorable market for fast food. I notice that the wealthiest nations are among the most middling data points, implying that as countries reach the highest wealth echelon, their economic growth slows. This slowed growth yields stability, allowing a booming middle class that then allows individuals access to more expensive (and often healthier) food options. The poorest nations are usually those with the highest economic growth. Like population, as a nation moves from low to high, initial growth is rapid. During this transitional phase, the lower class is, for the first time, gaining access to greater diversity of food options, maybe even having the option to purchase food rather than grow it for the first time. Additionally, these nations often have massive metropolitan centers rife with poverty, a market environment perfect for the fast food sector to corner.

raw_comment: Wow! There was so much to notice and wonder with this graph! Once we understood what the scale and the colour-coding was telling us, we started to ask questions about individual countries which would really require more research to answer. For example we first noticed that Greece had decreased in fast food sales by about 25% even though they had high income status. Why the decrease? This prompted another student to ask about Morocco as it is low/middle income but with stable wealth and an average increase (25%) in Fast Food Sales. Once this student commented, we had an "ah ha" moment as we realized that the horizontal axis had a lot of information to offer us. We went back to Greece which we then realized had significantly  decreasing wealth. We wondered why this is and thought that this would require more understanding of the economic and political situation in the individual countries.  Students cued into Argentina which had an astounding 120% plus increase in Fast Food Sales. They wondered if the explosion  had to do with soccer or tourism or some other major political/economic change. We then zoned in on  the United States. We asked why the US had only average increase in Fast Food sales and average increase in wealth. We then realized that the reference point was 2010-2015 which meant that the US already had an amazing amount of Fast Food sales at that point already. One of our students felt that a catchy title might be "US Falling Behind in Fast Food Sales Growth"

Welcome to “What’s Going On in This Graph?” and the Wednesday moderation.  Today’s graph focuses on the change in fast-food sales and wealth by country around the world.  Think about how fast food affects customers.  Study the graph and, from 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions. (On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.) 

	What do you NOTICE in this graph? 

	What do you WONDER? What are you curious about?

	What’s GOING ON in this graph?
Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.  If your headline makes a claim, tell us what you noticed that supports your claim.

The questions are intended to build on one another, so try to answer them in order. Start with “I notice” and then “I wonder,” and end with the headline.

Then, read some responses. Click on "Reply" to an interesting response to get a discussion going. Learn different perspectives when you read what other students have to say about your response. 

We look forward to reading your discoveries.
